Yes. 

The story is rich with subtext that feels completely natural and deeply enriches the setting—specifically, the late-1990s gay community on the cruise ship in the wake of the AIDS epidemic. 

A prime example of character subtext is the "coded question" Clara asks her father: *"Are you going to be tired?"* On the surface, she is asking about his energy levels for the vacation, and he replies with a joke about the Carter Administration. However, the subtext—which the narrator explicitly notes is their way of speaking without saying the words—is a conversation about how close he is to dying. Similarly, when her father hides minuscule pieces of prime rib under his parsley at dinner, the surface action is a neat table habit, while the subtext reveals his severe loss of appetite and physical wasting, as well as his desire to protect his daughter and friends from worrying about him.

This subtext directly enriches the setting during the "White Party" scene. On the surface, it is a loud, exuberant dance party with six hundred men in white jeans and angel wings dancing under soap-flake snow. However, the subtext of the setting is one of survival, grief, and defiance. The narrator observes that "nobody here was taking the air in their lungs for granted" and that "the music was keeping the dark water outside the rails from coming in." Furthermore, when Richard tells Clara during their final dance, *"You're going to be fine, Clara. You know how to find your people,"* the subtext is a final goodbye; he is preparing her for life after his imminent death by showing her how chosen families care for one another. None of this feels forced; rather, the humor and camp on the surface make the underlying tragedy and love much more poignant.
